full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa, right, had a so-so day against the Colts on Wednesday, while Cooper Rush appeared to move ahead of Jack Strand in the battle for the No. 3 role. Justin Casterline / Getty Images
WESTFIELD, Ind. — Let’s start with something positive.
Atlanta Falcons running back Tyler Goodson has had a good training camp and looks to have locked up the No. 3 running back spot. Goodson led Atlanta with seven carries for 28 yards in Friday’s preseason opener and looked good again Wednesday in what was a homecoming of sorts in the first of two joint practices against the Indianapolis Colts.
Goodson, who grew up 20 minutes from the Falcons’ practice facility, spent the first three seasons of his career with the Colts before signing with Atlanta this offseason. He was the third running back in the rotation during team work and looked as explosive as anyone on the offense.
Given his success in the backfield and his spot as the main kick returner, Goodson appears to have built a lead over Nathan Carter for what likely will be the final running back spot on the 53-man roster. On top of that, Goodson’s clothing brand — RARE — began selling this month.
“Guys in the locker room are wearing it too, which is cool,” he said. “Sales have been going great.”
In addition to Goodson, the highlights for the Falcons on Wednesday included a long and leaping touchdown catch by Drake London, Zachariah Branch lowering his shoulder and knocking down a Colts defender and an improved run defense. The teams will have one more joint practice Thursday and then play a preseason game on Saturday.
Here are six other takeaways from Wednesday’s action:
The first-team offense still hasn’t clicked. Tua Tagovailoa was 8-of-13 passing in 11-on-11 work against the Colts on Wednesday, and the only ball that traveled farther than 9 yards was a jump ball touchdown to London, who did most of the work, making the catch over a defender and scampering the final 30 yards to the end zone. Tagovailoa was 3-for-3 in seven-on-seven work.
“There are some things we can clean up, but I thought it went pretty well,” Tagovailoa said. “Regardless of how close or how far we think we are, the work still needs to be put in at the end of the day.”
Tagovailoa threw a pick six in the final team period of the day and faulted himself for bad ball placement. Still, he said he is getting more comfortable in the offense and hopes to continue building rapport with the wide receiving corps.
“We’re continuing to grow, figuring out how guys run their routes,” he said. “(I want to get) them to communicate with me and not go to their coach. Like, ‘Hey, let’s talk to each other.’ That’s how we’re going to be able to go out there and feel comfortable.”
Quarterback Jack Strand’s absence from team work was notable. With Michael Penix Jr. still sidelined for 11-on-11 work, veteran Cooper Rush got all of the second-team work Wednesday while Strand only participated in individual drills.
Rush didn’t have much more success than Tagovailoa, but he may have supplanted Strand for the No. 3 spot. If Strand doesn’t get some second-team reps in Thursday’s practice, it’ll be a bad sign for the rookie UDFA.
Penix’s only real action of the day came in seven-on-seven work, during which he was 6-for-9 passing.
Starting left tackle Jake Matthews played only one series in 11-on-11 work before giving way to Michael Jerrell at that spot. Jerrell and Wanya Morris appear to be competing for the Falcons’ swing tackle spot.
Right tackle is in much better shape with the return of veteran Jawaan Taylor, who had a good day Wednesday while taking all of the first-team snaps. Taylor said after the workout that his absence from the first two weeks of training camp was the result of minor knee surgery he had in March. The seven-year veteran said the triceps injury that cost him five games last year is completely healed since the start of the year.
“It was a lot of fun,” he said. “(The Colts) have a great defense, a lot of great players. We just had fun out here competing. Just getting better every day. It’s going really well.”
The Falcons cornerbacks didn’t have a great day, but the run defense showed marked improvement after a bad start against the Denver Broncos in last week’s preseason game. Atlanta had multiple run stuffs against Jonathan Taylor and the Indianapolis starting offense.
“Friday night wasn’t up to our standards at all,” defensive tackle Brandon Dorlus said. “We watched the film, we locked in, we came out here and played with a different type of energy.”
With Bijan Robinson not able to fully flex his muscle due to the nature of Wednesday’s practices (players were not allowed to be tackled to the ground), London was clearly the best Falcon on the field — even if he only had a handful of catches, a one-hander on the sideline and the leaping grab that he took for the touchdown .
“I think it went really, really well,” London said. “Obviously, there is a lot of stuff to clean up, but we’re finding our way right now, and we’re paving it, and I really like where we’re at.”

full_text:
Bears coaches are confident they are unlocking a new level of production for quarterback Caleb Williams. Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
During a training camp practice last week, Caleb Williams and Colston Loveland connected on an eye-pleasing explosive completion, a shot over the middle during which the second-year Chicago Bears tight end showed off his catch radius with a leaping, arms-extended grab in traffic.
It was a beautiful play, the type of big gain that will soon create roars on game days. And while positive moments like that will never be admonished inside the Bears’ meeting rooms, they will still be coached.
With Ben Johnson’s unrelenting emphasis on ball location for his quarterbacks — and for Williams in particular — there have been instances throughout the past three weeks in which good enough hasn’t really been good enough and where the push for precision continues to be hammered home.
That is one byproduct of the bar Johnson has raised at Halas Hall, with a championship standard established and all evaluations being performed accordingly. No one is exempt. No detail is too small.
Johnson continues to help everyone in the organization understand how last year’s success — an NFC North title and a wild-card round playoff win — can be sustained. Williams, meanwhile, may be the engine of the whole thing, being coached with heavy demands.
In June, a month before training camp opened, we turned our lens toward the Bears’ starting quarterback and four other players who had to undergo an eye test on the runway to the regular season. Now with camp more than three weeks old and the Bears in Cincinnati for an important joint practice Thursday with the Bengals, we’re offering the updated progress report on that quintet.
Progress report: Incomplete — arrow pointing up.
Since the spring, quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett has noticed gradual improvement with Williams’ ball location, an encouraging sign as the Bears equip their franchise quarterback to boost his completion percentage and the overall production of the passing attack.
As much as anything, Barrett has loved Williams’ buy-in to exactly what the coaching staff wants and his understanding of why it’s important.
Last year, the drive for greater passing precision was sometimes met with slight pushback, with Williams either breezing past specific criticisms or pointing out when his pass catchers failed to bring in a ball they should have grabbed.
“I’d be like, ‘No doubt,’” Barrett said. “Like, ‘No doubt about it. I hear you.’”
Still, Barrett reiterated, the goal on every pass isn’t just to hit the target but to nail the bull’s-eye.
“Now Caleb’s like, ‘No, you’re right. I can put it in a better spot,’” Barrett said.
Barrett reflects fondly on his time as a player, with two seasons spent in New Orleans watching recently inducted Hall of Famer Drew Brees master the craft.
“I was fascinated,” Barrett said, “with how if the ball was slightly over a receiver’s head, Drew would be like, ‘Hey, I’ll get you a better ball.’ (The receiver) still caught it. But he would say, ‘I’ll get you a better ball.’ For me, as a young quarterback, it was like, ‘Man …’”
Again, the goal isn’t just completions. It’s completions that produce the maximum possible gain, which is why Bears coaches talk so much to all their quarterbacks about consistently delivering a “runner’s ball” that allows the recipient to go to work after the catch.
The Bears are confident they are unlocking a new level of production for Williams with the quarterback himself continuing to take ownership with ball location. During camp, it has been evident.
A year ago, Barrett would have his corrections ready for Williams.
I need you to get that ball up a bit.
Remember, that one needs to be outside.
“Now,” Barrett said, “he’s saying it before I say it.”
Here’s what we wrote in June, more than a month ahead of the team’s report date, as we looked ahead to Gordon attempting to put his injury-plagued 2025 season and interrupted spring behind him.
“We’re not just interested in seeing Gordon back at practice. We’re interested in seeing him on the field. Every day. With no physical setbacks. Flying around and making the impact he’s capable of.”
Here we are less than three weeks from the season opener and the Bears’ nickelback isn’t back at practice, isn’t on the field, isn’t past his latest physical setback and certainly isn’t flying around to elevate the defense.
The Bears have said a calf issue has kept Gordon on the physically unable to perform list since camp began. And when asked after Saturday’s preseason opener about a timetable for Gordon’s return, Johnson offered just one word: unknown.
Johnson was a little more expansive Tuesday, but barely. “There’s a plan,” Johnson said. “And he’s working toward the plan.”
Patience among the coaches seems to be dwindling. Johnson is big on trust and players earning that from both coaches and teammates through demonstrated on-field competence. In short, Gordon hasn’t built any trust in this camp and the “unknown” timetable for when he might factor into the Bears’ plans has grown increasingly concerning.
Progress report: Incomplete.
Until Aug. 6, Jones had been practicing with elevated confidence and it was showing. The strength and/or trust he lacked in his left leg a year ago — both during camp and through the first month of the regular season — had returned and there was a noticeable spike in his power and poise.
Said offensive line coach Dan Roushar: “He’s a better football player than what we started with last year. That’s for sure.”
But during one-on-one drills in the team’s eighth camp practice, Jones experienced discomfort in his knee, exited practice and wound up missing the next three practices plus all 11-on-11 work in a fourth.
This week, he is back and has a golden opportunity to seize the starting left tackle job for Week 1. But demonstrating confidence, consistency, power and precision will be paramount. The Bears hope to heavily test Jones during Thursday’s joint practice in Cincinnati.
Johnson has made it clear one of his top wishes for the starting left tackle is the ability to be regularly sturdy in one-on-one pass protection. In the run game, Roushar has identified the need for Jones to play with better pad level and use his lower half to help attack defenders in space.
“I have to get him to run off the football better and see the target line,” Roushar said. “Then he has to be able to accelerate and stay in control of the block. We’re just not as consistent as we need to be.”
The next two weeks offer a great time for Jones to meet his coaches’ demands and continue playing with self-belief.
Arguably the best play of Odunze’s camp to date was a 10-yard touchdown reception made during an end-of-half period on Aug. 8, a third-down catch on an extended play with Odunze going up in the back of the end zone to snatch a fastball from Williams, then twisting his body to get both feet down.
“It was a last-second play,” Odunze said. “We needed it. The play broke down and it was a last-ditch effort. Thankfully, Caleb put the ball up to give me an opportunity. And I was able to come down with it.”
Added offensive coordinator Press Taylor: “There have been a number of those I can think of off the top of my head (with Rome). … That goes back to his college tape; that was a strength of his. So we’re just trying to kind of lean in and see how that fits our offense.”
After 15 camp practices, Odunze has 15 made positive deposits into his 2026 development bank. And if there were any concerns that the foot injuries that limited him last season and eventually caused him to miss the final five regular-season games would linger, they have disintegrated.
“I don’t think about it honestly,” Odunze said Tuesday.
Added receivers coach Antwaan Randle El: “I don’t see anything (adverse). And I’m always looking.”
Instead, Odunze has been working to become a more well-rounded receiver. Since the spring, he has shown flashes…

title: The Cowboys offense looks totally original again. Meet the man helping design it Klayton Adams wants his offense to be creative and complex, physical and unpredictable, to break rules but still feel realistic. Jourdan Rodrigue

OXNARD, Calif. — At Yard House, a busy chain restaurant just outside of the Dallas Cowboys’ training camp facility in Southern California, a dream sequence for a football dork is unfolding: Creed’s “With Arms Wide Open” plays over the speakers as offensive coordinator Klayton Adams talks about run-game design.

full_text:
After a successful debut, Klayton Adams is entering his second season as the Cowboys' offensive coordinator. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; James D. Smith / AP
OXNARD, Calif. — At Yard House, a busy chain restaurant just outside of the Dallas Cowboys’ training camp facility in Southern California, a dream sequence for a football dork is unfolding: Creed’s “With Arms Wide Open” plays over the speakers as offensive coordinator Klayton Adams talks about run-game design.
Specifically, Adams is fascinated by what happens to a defense when the run strength of an offensive formation changes suddenly and at high speed. Some teams have tight ends (or even receivers) quickly sift from the outside of the formation into the middle gaps as the ball is snapped. For the running back, it’s like a miner using a smaller dynamite blast to clear rubble before the big sticks are used. For the defenders, it either moves a gap or creates a new one to think about in their assignments. Their math problem changes at the latest possible time.
“I think (it’s good) any time you’re messing with people’s eyes,” said Adams. “You’re still dealing with human beings.”
Adams likes that when these plays are drawn on a card, they feel “messy on paper.” Everyone wants their run drawings to look nice, he said, but on the play card they feel static. He wants his to feel alive. Just as the passing game should, Adams wants the run game to attack every area of a defense, not just what is in front of the offensive line. These days, such concepts have to do more . So do the Cowboys.
Dallas head coach Brian Schottenheimer called Adams, then the Arizona Cardinals’ offensive line coach, in the 2025 offseason while Adams and one of his three daughters were in the car on a drive to Las Vegas. They talked for so long — and Adams became so excited — that when Adams finally hung up the phone, his daughter turned to him from the passenger seat and asked, “So, are we moving again?”
In his first season as offensive coordinator, Adams, 43, helped lead the Cowboys offense into genuinely exciting territory. In 2025, Dallas finished No. 5 in EPA per play, second in yards per game and No. 7 in scoring (27.7 points per game); the offense scored on nearly half of its drives, which ranked second in the NFL.
The way the offense operated drew even more attention. These were not the typical Dallas Cowboys. Schottenheimer paired his West Coast passing concepts with Adams’ physical, diverse run scheme to create a system that was modern in its finesse and explosiveness and also a gritty throwback. Dallas uses motions and shifts in both the run and the pass game; their rushing attack features powerful gap concepts but also layered, stretching zone runs. They change formations before and at the snap. The Cowboys play fast — their passing game weaponizes pace. They want to chew up all of the grass on the field.
They were explosive — No. 7 in explosive plays in 2025 — and want to be even more so in the run game this year, as Adams’ system typically has been. Quarterback Dak Prescott was terrific in this offense, which featured two 1,000-plus-yard receivers, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens; a 1,200-yard rusher in Javonte Williams; and a combined 1,075 receiving yards from Jake Ferguson (TE1) and Ryan Flournoy (WR3).
If not for the deadweight anchor of their league-worst defense, the Cowboys might have realized a far higher potential than their 7-9-1 record suggested.
The 2025 season was enough proof of concept for Schottenheimer and Adams to lean even further into what is working. And what is working can sometimes be a little alternative in theory. Adams got a lot of buy-in from players in Arizona, and the Cardinals had the NFL’s fifth-highest rushing success rate in 2024, ahead of rushing powerhouses like the Los Angeles Rams, Buffalo Bills and Philadelphia Eagles.
His job was to make the seemingly complex more realistic — to show players and fellow coaches how some of his creativity could translate into a physical, multiple running game that presents many different looks to a defense while keeping the intent of the play simple for his own offensive players.
“He knows that it’ll make things easier if we show (the defense) a different picture and still get to what we really want to get to,” said Cowboys starting guard Tyler Booker. “The key to offense is doing the same thing over and over again but making it look like 18 different things.”
It is indeed creative, perhaps more so than you’d initially expect from an offensive coordinator with an O-line background. Booker, laughing, said that everything they’ve gotten into so far has been “within reason.” It typically takes five to seven weeks for an offense to fully understand what it will be that season. By about Week 9 last year, Adams said the Cowboys were all-in.
“He’s a joy to play for,” said Booker, “because you know he’s gonna make you better.
“We’re very creative. We’re not one-dimensional. … We have the capability to run anything we want, to attack a defense’s weaknesses.”
Adams was a run-game coordinator early in his career at Division II Western Washington, a school at which the football team no longer exists. There, his Vikings kept everything on the table schematically.
“The players wanted to do cool things, and it’s not like there were 80,000 people there that were gonna throw rocks at you after the game,” Adams said. “I just felt like it was a really safe environment to break some rules and throw the rattle out of the crib, you know?
“I’ve kind of hung on to that a little bit.”
Adams draws inspiration from everywhere — the spacing and set pieces of soccer (his daughters play in a competitive club league); the “explosives” reel composed of every other team’s run plays of 10-plus yards and pass plays of 20-plus yards each week; his “cool sh–” file of plays gathered from every level of football . Adams once even got some ideas for a practice workflow from a gymnastics coach at a college where he coached.
“He studies so much film; I don’t think I’m ever in his office when he’s not just grinding on film and looking for advantages and edges,” Schottenheimer said.
“I try to be very curious. I’ve always been that way,” said Adams, smiling. “I wouldn’t say that I’m, like, really, really bright by any means. But I know when I see something that is a different color than something else, and I need to figure out what it is.”
He starts his play design and even game plans with “things that bother him” about the opponent. He tries to figure out “what will make those things not bother him.”
“I’m trying to do something (schematically), and they’re making it really hard,” he explained. “Here’s my folder of ‘things that hurt that.’ Because every danger has opportunity in it. If I think of things that way, I feel like I find solutions faster.”
This year, Adams is also installing the passing game for Dallas — a new challenge with high expectations, considering he is presenting to Prescott and the star receivers in meetings — but both Adams and Schottenheimer are pleased with how it’s gone so far. “It’s kind of good for me to listen,” said Schottenheimer, “because it makes my creative juices get going.”
Adams believes in installing an enormous amount of volume into his offense — the Cowboys will build a large library of concepts with players in training camp and then call back to them and add wrinkles throughout the season — because that means he has more flexibility within his scheme and can prevent the identity of the group from staying too rigid. An offense will naturally become different versions of itself as the season progresses; Adams feels he must change with it.
True leadership, he thinks, is a combination of elite problem-solving and influence.
“I want to give the players real solutions. I want them to go, ‘Yeah, I can’t wait until we call that play,’” he said. “I think there are so many ways that great coaches can simplify something that looks very complex.…

full_text:
Brenton Cox Jr. sacks Steelers quarterback Mason Rudolph in the Packers' first preseason game. Justin K. Aller / Getty Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Some fans undoubtedly had flashbacks when Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur announced on Tuesday that he planned to start quarterback Jordan Love on Friday night in Denver.
It was in Denver last year that the Packers’ season fell apart. They entered that game with a 9-3-1 record, sitting atop the NFC North and with the conference’s No. 2 seed.
They left Denver that day having lost their best offensive lineman, Zach Bako-Bewele, for the rest of the season to a partially torn patellar tendon. Wide receiver Christian Watson spent part of that afternoon in the hospital getting checked for dislocated ribs after falling awkwardly on a deep ball that cornerback Patrick Surtain II intercepted with the Packers leading by nine in the third quarter. Not only did that lead evaporate and the Packers lose two key offensive players for the remainder of the game, but their best player, edge Micah Parsons, tore his ACL and is still about two months out from playing in a game.
The Packers didn’t win again, losing five in a row to end their season. Those inside 1265 Lombardi Ave. can only hope they avoid a similar house of horrors in their second preseason game.
We know Love and other healthy prominent players will see time, but here are five other players to keep an eye on Friday night based on what we’ve seen throughout training camp.
I had Cox on my list of players to watch entering the Packers’ Family Night practice two weeks ago, and he continues making plays. During Wednesday’s shorter, toned-down practice that was closed to the public, Cox cleanly beat right tackle Dalton Cooper to pressure quarterback Kyle McCord and, not long after, stuffed running back MarShawn Lloyd on a toss left by beating him to the perimeter. Cox then blew by right tackle Anthony Belton with the twos to get in quarterback Tyrod Taylor’s face. There might be more flashy names fans are relying on to step up in Micah Parsons’ absence, behind Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Dani Dennis-Sutton and Collin Oliver among them, but don’t forget that Cox has been here longer than them and had a productive four sacks in seven games two years ago before missing most of last season with a groin injury.
“I know when I’m attacking, I’m hard to stop,” Cox said. “Nobody wants their face peeled off every play like that, so when I’m attacking, it’s either I’m going to peel your face off, or you might get me, but I’m coming back to you.”
Hadden said Wednesday that he isn’t sure if he’ll play Friday in Denver — he didn’t play last Thursday against the Steelers — but it would be a promising step for the 25-year-old cornerback if he did. Hadden returned to practice on Aug. 2 from the PUP list after breaking his tibia and fibula and dislocating his ankle in Week 17 last season. On Wednesday, he repped with the No. 1 defense in the slot (he was formerly an outside corner) with defensive back Javon Bullard sidelined with a foot injury, a testament to what coaches think of him as a depth piece, even if he may not be game-ready just yet. Hadden picked off McCord on Wednesday after McCord threw a play-action bootleg into traffic and celebrated accordingly with teammates all the way down the field.
“I’m definitely going to play before the end of camp, definitely going to play, but whatever I can do, I’m pushing for it,” Hadden said. “I’m ready to be back out there. I’m ready to prove to myself, but also want to prove to my brothers and teammates and to this organization that I’m still me, and I’m back, and I’m better. It’d mean a lot to get back out there and perform.”
Ford threw running back Jaden Nixon to the ground so aggressively during Tuesday’s practice that left tackle Jordan Morgan got in his face and shoved him. Granted, it’s not that remarkable a feat since Ford is listed at 6 feet 5 inches and 338 pounds, while Nixon is listed at 5-10 and 199 pounds, but it was another notable play in what has been an impressive camp for Ford. The mammoth defensive tackle was a Packers seventh-round pick in 2022 and spent his first three years in Green Bay before signing with the Chicago Bears off the Packers’ practice squad in December 2024. The Packers then claimed him off waivers from the Bears last December, and he’s now seeing snaps with the first-team defense.
“I see a guy that’s really matured as not only a football player but as a person,” LaFleur said. “He is a load inside, and he’s done a really nice job playing the nose position and defeating blocks. He’s been pretty impactful throughout camp.”
The rookie fifth-round pick from Kentucky still appears to be competing for a starting spot. Though veteran left guard Aaron Banks’ return to 11-on-11 work has moved Burton to a backup role, he still got reps with the first string at right guard on Wednesday despite working at left guard with the second string. With Belton’s regression and weaknesses in pass protection relegating him to the backup right tackle, the starting right guard spot seems to be a competition between Jacob Monk (currently leading) and Burton. Burton may see time at both guard positions on Friday night, given the Packers’ preference for their reserve interior offensive linemen to play at least three spots.
“I’m not going to sit and lie. That’s everyone’s goal here,” Burton said of his desire to start. “You want to be on the field. It’s a different thing being on the field versus not. But at the end of the day, I’m going to do whatever helps win the Packers football games, so whatever role that is, I’m excited for it.”
It seems like Sturdivant makes an impressive catch every day. Not just a routine one, but a grab that makes you wonder how hard it’ll be for the Packers to keep him off the 53-man roster. On Wednesday, he hauled in a bomb from McCord on a deep corner route over safety Tra Fluellen for the most impressive connection of the day.
“He’s been doing that all camp,” McCord said. “Creating separation.”
The Packers have had an undrafted rookie on their Week 1 roster for 21 straight seasons. If anyone continues that streak this year, it’ll probably be Sturdivant, though his inclusion might require the Packers to keep seven receivers instead of six. Another strong showing in Denver for the 6-foot-3, 207-pound receiver could make their decision that much more difficult.

full_text:
New Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen Mykal McEldowney / Imagn Images
WESTFIELD, Ind. — Keenan Allen didn’t need a middleman, at least not initially. The trust between the veteran wide receiver and Indianapolis Colts coach Shane Steichen was built years ago during a seven-season stint together with the Chargers. They’d kept in touch even after parting ways, including this offseason, when their conversations slowly shifted from catching up to possibly catching passes from Colts quarterback Daniel Jones.
“It’s been a little bit of back and forth,” Allen said Wednesday during his introductory news conference. “Just me and (Steichen) personally — without the agent.”
Allen kept the specific timeline of his conversations with Steichen private, though it’s no secret his fondness for the coach was a big factor in his decision to join the Colts. Of course, an agent was eventually roped in when Indianapolis landed Allen on a one-year deal .
Allen said he had other suitors, which he did not disclose, but the chance to reunite with Steichen was too good an opportunity to pass up. They’ve always worked well together, evidenced by four of Allen’s six Pro Bowl nods occurring when Steichen was on the Chargers’ coaching staff. For two of those seasons, 2019 and 2020, Steichen served as the Chargers’ offensive coordinator. The result: Allen totaled 2,191 receiving yards, 14 touchdowns and 204 receptions — trailing only former Houston Texans star DeAndre Hopkins for the most catches in the league during that span.
“He’s a genius,” Allen said of Steichen. “… He knows the game. He knows the ins and outs, and the way that he knows the game, I know the game, as well. That’s kind of how I was raised in the NFL world.”
It’s been six years since Allen and Steichen were on the same team, but despite all the time that’s passed, Allen believes they won’t miss a beat mentally or, perhaps more importantly for the 14-year veteran, physically. Last year, Allen collected 777 yards and four touchdowns on 81 catches with the Chargers, the most receptions by any receiver age 33 or older in the NFL. Asked how he’s continued to get open at this stage of his career, Allen joked that it wasn’t because of any next-level physical trait.
“Starting off, my rookie year, I was slow,” said the now 34-year-old Allen, who ran a 4.71-second 40-yard dash during his pro day in 2013. “So, I guess I haven’t lost no speed.”
Steichen gave Allen a little more credit. After all, he is one of just 18 players in NFL history who have tallied 1,000 receptions. In fact, Allen is only 16 catches away from passing Colts legend and current wide receivers coach Reggie Wayne for the 11th-most catches in NFL history.
“The way he plays, and the feel he has for the game … he’s the most cerebral receiver I’ve ever been around,” Steichen said. “He sees the game like a quarterback. How to run routes, how to attack leverage, how he sees coverage … He’s seen so many different looks, and it’s like clockwork for him in his brain, so having that at that position as you get older, really helps you in the long run.”
Steichen said he wasn’t worried about how Allen will fit in with the rest of the Colts’ pass catchers, led by the trio of Alec Pierce, Josh Downs and Tyler Warren. Warren is entering his second season in Indy after notching the third-most receiving yards (817) by a rookie tight end in franchise history in 2025. Pierce and Downs headline the Colts’ receiver room, with Allen likely slotting in as the team’s third starting wideout. He’s poised to replace Michael Pittman Jr., who led the Colts in catches four of the past five years before Indy traded him to the Pittsburgh Steelers in the spring.
When pressed further on the potential redundancy of Allen and Downs in particular, since both have thrived in the slot, Steichen again pushed back on any issues. Allen led the NFL with 34 receptions on third down last year, with 29 turning into first downs. Of Downs’ 21 third-down receptions last year, the most of any Colts player, 20 accounted for first downs. From Steichen’s perspective, Indy’s offense can only benefit by adding another player known for moving the chains.
joint practice reps🤝 pic.twitter.com/eblM1v5Nbm
— Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 19, 2026
“We’re gonna try (different) ways to win every game,” Steichen said. “However that happens (is what we’ll do). … Both of those guys are really talented. All four of the guys we talked about earlier (Allen, Downs, Pierce and Warren), we’re excited about all those skill sets.”
Jones echoed his coach, saying he can’t wait to share the field with Allen. The QB won’t have to wait long, since Allen said he plans to participate in the Colts’ second joint practice with the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday, which will be the Colts’ last training camp practice this year.
“He’s played with a lot of really good quarterbacks,” Jones said of Allen. “I think from what I’ve heard and from just talking to him a little bit, I know he’s a smart football player, very aware and studies the game. … Looking forward to getting with him and learning kind of how he sees it.”
The Falcons had the Colts’ number in the run game Wednesday, stuffing Indy’s star running back Jonathan Taylor a few times behind the line of scrimmage. But it was a different story through the air. Jones finished 15-of-15 passing in 11-on-11 drills, highlighted by a 65-yard touchdown to Downs.
“I feel good moving around,” said Jones, who is more than eight months removed from having surgery to repair his ruptured right Achilles. “I think with any major rehab process, you’re always kind of progressing and getting back and getting used to doing everything. … There’s nothing I don’t feel good doing.”
Colts cornerback Justin Walley picked off Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa in an 11-on-11 session and returned it for a touchdown. The pass was intended for Falcons star receiver Drake London, but Walley read Tagovailoa’s eyes and jumped the route perfectly. Walley, a second-year pro, has primarily played in the slot during training camp, but he started on the outside Wednesday in place of Charvarius Ward Sr., who remains sidelined due to a back injury. Veteran Cam Taylor-Britt replaced Walley in the slot.
“Walley’s a playmaker, and it’s great to have him back coming off the (ACL) injury,” Steichen said. “He’s been making plays all camp, and to see that, I was really excited for him.”
it’s Walley’s world. pic.twitter.com/PooS119FUf
— Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 19, 2026
Steichen did not have an update on Ward, who was present at practice but did not participate. Ward hasn’t practiced since Aug. 9 due to a back injury. Asked if Ward could need surgery, Steichen said, “I don’t think so, no.”
Steichen confirmed that Warren suffered a groin injury in Wednesday’s practice. The standout tight end fell while running a route in 11-on-11s, and when he got up, he began clutching at his right groin. Warren was checked by the team’s medical staff, and they eventually wrapped the injured area with an ice pack.
Finally, Steichen provided a positive update on Pierce. The Colts’ top receiver has not practiced this offseason, as he continues rehabbing from left ankle and heel surgery.
“Alec’s in a great spot right now,” Steichen said. “He’s doing really good. I watched him work out (Tuesday) in the indoor (practice facility). He’s moving around really good, so hopefully we’ll have him back sooner than later.”
Steichen added that Indy’s deal with Allen was completely independent of Pierce’s recovery timeline. The Colts expect both players to be on the field together in their season opener against the Baltimore Ravens on Sept. 13.

full_text:
The Seahawks are the reigning NFC champions, but Austin Mock's NFL Projection Model doesn't see them winning the conference again this year. Ronald Martinez / Getty Images
My NFL Projection Model doubted the Seattle Seahawks last year and looked foolish. And did it learn its lesson? Nope!
While my model is projecting a far better season for Seattle than the 8.6 wins it forecast last year, it doesn’t believe the reigning Super Bowl champs are going back-to-back.
Instead, the model is hopping aboard the Los Angeles Rams bandwagon after the Seahawks’ NFC West rival made some major splashes this offseason, trading for reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and star cornerback Trent McDuffie to bolster their defense. Honestly, the model isn’t really slighting Seattle, forecasting the Seahawks to win the second-most games in the NFC and third-most in the NFL.
But that’s not to say it’s a two-horse race in the NFC. The model projects three more teams to finish with 10-plus wins, and a few more to win at least nine. So, while the NFC is not quite as wide-open as the AFC, there are still several teams with a realistic shot at making the playoffs and winning the Super Bowl.
Like we did yesterday for the AFC , let’s examine the odds before diving into each division.
Just two years ago, the Philadelphia Eagles were kings of the NFL after throttling the Kansas City Chiefs in the Super Bowl; 18 months later, their hold on the NFC East — a division they’ve won two years in a row — feels tenuous. Wide receiver A.J. Brown is gone , and while DeVonta Smith can step into his shoes as the offense’s No. 1, not having a pair of star pass catchers could be tough for Jalen Hurts.
If the Eagles’ quarterback struggles again this season, real questions will be asked about his future as the franchise’s starting quarterback. Perhaps a change at offensive coordinator — Hurts is used to those by now — will help the QB return to form. Even though Sean Mannion is young and inexperienced, my model thinks he’ll spark the offense. And even if it doesn’t, the defense has a chance to be elite again, which gives Philly a leg up to win this division for a third straight time.
The Dallas Cowboys are the NFC’s Cincinnati Bengals. And by that, I mean the model is confident the offense will be great, but the defense is a much bigger question. The Cowboys’ defense improved in the second half of last season after the team traded for defensive tackle Quinnen Williams; they’ve since added pass rushers Rashan Gary (trade), Von Miller (free agency) and Malachi Lawrence (first round of the draft) to form a potentially formidable front alongside Donovan Ezeiruaku. And, of course, the Cowboys spent their other first-round pick on do-it-all defensive back Caleb Downs. If the young players can thrive in a system that revolves around Williams and boost Dallas’ defense, that will give QB Dak Prescott and company a high ceiling.
The Washington Commanders and New York Giants aren’t hopeless, but the model sees their rosters as significantly weaker than those of the Eagles and Cowboys. Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels and New York’s Jaxson Dart must stay healthy and take the next step for either of these teams to be contenders. Washington added a handful of solid veterans in free agency to bolster the defense, so that will be worth monitoring. As for the Giants, can new head coach John Harbaugh raise this team’s floor ? If so, how high?
The model is calling its worst-to-first shot right here. The Detroit Lions finished last in the NFC North last year at 9-8, but my model sees them as the favorites this year, and that’s primarily because of a favorable schedule. Per my model, the Lions play the 29th-easiest schedule in the league, which is expected to give them an extra half win over their rivals.
The Green Bay Packers are perhaps the toughest team to project this year, with a wide range of possible outcomes. Star pass rusher Micah Parsons will be out for at least the first month of the season. Without him last year, the Packers ranked 28th in EPA per play; they were 15th with him on the field. I like new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon, but is there enough for him to work with? A similar question could be asked for coach Matt LaFleur’s offense . He’s good, but there are some major issues on that offensive line, and I could see the bottom falling out for this offense if QB Jordan Love lacks adequate protection.
The NFC North is tricky! The Chicago Bears are another team that’s tough to decipher. All eyes are on Caleb Williams and whether he can improve his down-to-down consistency this season. Yes, the Bears won the division in 2025, but Williams finished outside the top 20 in dropback EPA and dropback success rate. If that doesn’t improve, I have little faith in a defense that’s likely to take a step back after relying heavily on creating turnovers last year.
The Minnesota Vikings are projected to finish last, but they are getting a big upgrade at quarterback with Kyler Murray. I’m not sure if Murray is a top-10 quarterback, but I’m confident he can play at that level for stretches, even if he ends up being closer to average. That’s still a huge improvement over what they got from their quarterbacks last year. Pair average quarterback play with those receivers and defensive coordinator Brian Flores, and you’re going to find yourself in the playoff hunt more often than not.
An 8-9 record topped the NFC South last year, and my model forecasts a similar outcome this year, with no team in the division projected to win more than eight games.
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are favored to win the division, but they’re old, and their quarterback, Baker Mayfield, is unhappy that he hasn’t signed an extension yet. Perhaps Mayfield will use that as motivation and deliver a big season. If he doesn’t, though, maybe he’s not Tampa’s QB next season. Meanwhile, the New Orleans Saints are right behind them, but they just lost their first-round wide receiver Jordyn Tyson to another hamstring injury, so he’s going on the shelf for a bit. New Orleans also lost underrated defensive tackle Bryan Bresee earlier in camp.
The Atlanta Falcons already look like they’re in trouble at QB , as Michael Penix Jr. doesn’t look like he’ll be ready for the start of the season and there are now questions about Tua Tagovailoa’s health for Week 1. Yes, Bijan Robinson, Drake London and Kyle Pitts are an awesome trio of playmakers, but if no one can get them the ball consistently, how much can they do?
And then there’s the first-to-worst Carolina Panthers. That’s right, a year after they “conquered” the division at 8-9, my model forecasts a division-worst 6.7 wins for the Panthers in 2026. That’s partially because of a difficult schedule, but mostly because the model isn’t a fan of quarterback Bryce Young, especially if his offensive line isn’t healthy. Remember, they lost left tackle Ikem Ekwonu to a knee injury late last year, and right tackle Taylor Moton is out for an extended period with a blood clot in his lung.
My model already loved the Rams, so it’s no surprise that after adding Garrett and McDuffie, Los Angeles is projected to be the best team in the NFL. But even being the odds-on favorite this season only gives them a 14 percent chance to win the Super Bowl, as they play in an incredibly tough division and have the league’s third-toughest schedule.
The Seahawks look to repeat as Super Bowl champions, and if they do, we’ll start having serious conversations about head coach Mike Macdonald and his place in history (the next Bill Belichick?). If he can keep this defense elite after losing some key players in free agency, it will be impressive. My bigger concerns for Seattle, however, come on offense. Former offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak left to become head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders, and the Seahawks are turning over play-calling duties to an unknown commodity in Brian Fleury. It’s also worth noting that…

full_text:
Giants linebacker Abdul Carter tackles quarterback J.J. McCarthy during Saturday's preseason loss to the Vikings. Rich Graessle / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. – Abdul Carter has an ambitious goal he is not afraid to share. In fact, he has already shared it privately with his New York Giants teammates.
“I want to be the greatest of all time,” he told The Athletic .
“I mean the greatest of all time,” Carter replied, “in terms of just a football player in general.”
He was standing tall inside the Giants’ practice facility, still sweating in practice gear that included full pads, a blue hoodie and a white jersey carrying his new number, 3. Carter spent his first NFL season wearing No. 51 after Lawrence Taylor rejected the rookie’s bid to unretire his iconic No. 56.
A post shared by Zone 🗽| #GiantsPride (@giantszone_)
If LT wanted the kid to establish his own identity, guess what? Carter has every intention of doing just that.
“When (John) Harbaugh first got here, everybody had to go in front of the room and speak, and I told everybody that I want to be the greatest of all time,” Carter told The Athletic . “And I can’t just say that. I’ve got to come out here and work and prove it during games this season. I’ve got to be that player.”
As everybody’s All-American out of Penn State and the No. 3 pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, Carter did not show that consistent level of commitment in Year 1, twice getting himself benched by interim coach Mike Kafka for missing team activities. But Harbaugh and others in the Giants organization have raved about Carter’s professionalism this time around — in the meeting room, in the locker room, on the practice field, you name it.
“Abdul is practicing at the highest level,” Harbaugh said. “His effort, intensity, skill set — he’s excelling every day. He looks great, and I can’t wait to see him play.”
It’s early in Year 2, very early, but the 6-foot-3, 252-pound linebacker was described by one team source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak candidly about Carter, as “a man on a mission.” Carter had already put his short-term mission on the record earlier in camp when he said, “I want to be Defensive Player of the Year.”
But at age 22, Carter also embraces the long-term possibilities for a pass rusher with his size, strength and speed. Though he managed only four sacks in 2025, Carter delivered a strong finish and led the league with 48 quick pressures (within 2.5 seconds of the snap), per Next Gen Stats.
“To be honest, everybody wants the sacks, so I’m not sitting here and saying I don’t care about them,” Carter said. “But sacks are a little bit overrated. Every time you rush, you’re not going to get a sack. It’s all about affecting the quarterback and affecting the guy who touches the ball every play. As long as I can keep doing that and nobody does it faster, I’ll keep that up and the sacks are going to come along with that.”
Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has said Carter is spending the summer “mastering the technique and fundamentals” of his craft in an attempt to become far more than an overpowering athlete on the edge. Carter agrees with this assessment. He said he now realizes he’ll become a better playmaker if he becomes a better craftsman.
But Carter’s natural instinct will likely remain his most lethal weapon. Giants radio analyst Carl Banks, a two-time Super Bowl champ from the Bill Parcells days, suggested as much with this quote-tweet of a video showing Carter shedding two blockers and tackling J.J. McCarthy in Saturday’s preseason loss to Minnesota:
“Not many can do what Carter does here and kids don’t try it and coaches don’t try to teach … He literally goes underneath 2 blocks and still makes a tackle for loss … This is the sh*t LT would do. Defied the laws of leverage.”
Not many can do what Carter does here and kids dont try ot and Coaches dont try to teach.. He literally goes underneath 2 blocks and still make a tackle for loss..
This is the sh*t LT would do.  Defied the laws of leverage https://t.co/yJuEE0vVDC
— Carl Banks (@CarlBanksGIII) August 17, 2026
Banks isn’t one to compare anyone or anything to his old teammate, Taylor, but the last linebacker the Giants drafted as early as they drafted Carter (Banks was selected No. 3 in 1984) posted what he posted.
“Abdul does things naturally,” Banks said by phone. “He just does it. … If you asked him, ‘What did you do on that play?’ he probably couldn’t tell you. And that’s the stuff LT used to do. ‘I don’t know. I just made the play.’ … There are probably only three or four other guys who could’ve made that play.”
Banks criticized Carter on WFAN Radio last year after his second benching, saying, “It’s time for the kid to grow up.”
This year? “I think he figured it out,” Banks said.
Asked about the former linebacker’s praise on social media and the comparison to Taylor, Carter said, “I’ve actually got a lot of respect for Carl Banks, LT, Harry Carson, all those guys. I go back and watch the full games of when they played in the ’80s and early ’90s. I actually try to mimic some of the things they did, just the violence they played with, just the recklessness. So that’s a pretty big compliment and I appreciate that.”
Truth is, Harbaugh wants the Giants to look and play like the glory-days Giants. That connection seems obvious at the linebacker position, on the outside and inside with Carter, Brian Burns, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese, the fifth pick in the 2026 NFL Draft.
Carter expects to emerge as the best member of that group. He feels a responsibility to emerge as the best player on the team.
“I absolutely feel that way, and I told (Jaxson) Dart the same thing,” Carter said. “In order for us to be who we want to be and add another banner in this place, we have to be the best players.”
Carter said Dart replied, “We’re on the same page.”
Of course, they weren’t even in the same library in May, after the linebacker blitzed his quarterback on social media for introducing President Donald Trump at a suburban New York rally. In his first news conference afterward, Carter was most impressive in how he stood on his principles without causing irreparable harm to a valued teammate and friend.
Now Carter needs Dart to play at a very high level, and Dart needs Carter to become the historic figure Carter hopes to be.
“There’s a reason that I asked for No. 56 when I did,” Carter said. “My whole thing is I just want to go out and show my teammates and show this city why I asked for that number.
“We’ve had some great, great players in this league, and I want my name mentioned when you say, ‘OK, who’s the greatest player of all time, especially on the defensive side of the ball?’ I want to be mentioned with LT, Bruce Smith, Aaron Donald, all those guys.”
If nothing else, Abdul Carter is not at all afraid of the Giant effort it will take to get there.

full_text:
Will Howard led an impressive two-minute drill in the Steelers' preseason opener. David Dermer / AP
PITTSBURGH, Pa. — From the press box overlooking the playing field, Steelers assistant general manager Andy Weidl watched the young quarterback lead the two-minute drill. A gutsy fourth-down completion moved the chains. A well-timed screen gained critical chunk yardage. Then, a crisp throw between the split safeties set the table at the 1-yard line.
As the touchdown drive unfolded, Weidl found himself thinking back to the 2025 college football playoff — and all the moments during Ohio State’s National Championship run that made him a Will Howard believer.
“(Howard) picked himself off the mat after the Ohio State-Michigan game when they lost at home,” Weidl said on Wednesday. “He played his best football at the most important time in the playoffs. He elevated his team. He elevated his play. The moment was never too big. He was poised, much like we saw the other night in the two-minute drill.”
On Friday, Howard will once again be asked to meet the moment. He will start the Steelers’ second game of the preseason, taking on the New York Jets. Rookie Drew Allar is scheduled to play the remainder of the game, while veterans Aaron Rodgers and Mason Rudolph sit out.
The buzz may surround Allar after his splashy, three-touchdown debut . But in a four-man room full of storylines and intrigue, Howard truly is the key variable — the player who could swing this entire conversation in one direction or the other, with possible ripple effects up and down the depth chart.
“I just want to show the fanbase and myself and everybody that I’m capable of playing at this level,” Howard said. “Just continue to show that progression and growth.”
The way that coach Mike McCarthy is approaching this game has appropriately framed the current competition. Rodgers is QB1; that’s the easy part. Allar made the 53-man roster the minute the Steelers used a third-round pick on him last spring. And while Rudolph’s spot as QB2 isn’t quite written in pen, nothing he does in a preseason game is going to alter anyone’s opinion of a player who is entering his ninth NFL season.
“I saw what I needed to see from Mason last week,” McCarthy said.
That’s what makes Howard such an important piece of this entire conversation. Will they keep three QBs or four? Is Rudolph locked in as QB2 or could he be had for the right price in a trade? Longer term, can Howard prove he should be part of a 2027 QB competition? Or is Howard a cut or trade candidate himself?
The possibilities span the spectrum. There’s a scenario in which Howard closes the significant lead that Rudolph built to become QB2. There’s another one where Howard falls down the depth chart or off of the 53-man roster entirely. Somewhere in between, the Steelers could play for right now by keeping Rudolph and also for the future by retaining Howard in a rare four-QB room.
“It’s me versus me every single day,” Howard said. “I’m just trying to get better every single day.”
When you realize how many possibilities and hypotheticals hinge upon how Howard performs, his somewhat cliche quote really is an apt way to describe this whole situation. For so many of the QB questions, Howard is the only one who can provide the answer.
On Wednesday, Howard took a minute to break down his debut. In the three-series outing that McCarthy described as “peaks and valleys,” Howard completed seven of nine passes for 86 yards and a QB rating of 106.5.
“I think the two-minute drive was great,” Howard said. “I think we executed really well and did a good job of not letting a fourth down early in the drive stop us, and then compiling a couple big plays.”
On the flip side, Howard acknowledged that he felt a little “antsy” in the pocket on the first drive. He said an emphasis in this game will be to continue through his progressions and not “flee too early.” The second-year signal caller also pointed out when he put the ball in harm’s way on the final third down.
“Just being smart with the football, keeping the ball out of jeopardy,” Howard said. “The last third down that I had, I kind of threw it back over the middle. Obviously, nothing (bad) happened. But you just don’t want to practice bad habits.”
McCarthy said he’d like Howard to get off to a better start than he did in the first preseason game. The coach also acknowledged that a couple of the miscues weren’t on Howard. On one play, a receiver ran the wrong route. On another, a missed assignment up front led to a free rusher.
“A couple of those plays weren’t really his fault,” McCarthy said. “But you’ve got to react to negative situations … I thought he did.”
One of the toughest things for Howard to navigate during this process will be to rise to the occasion without pressing. Before he’s asked to step in and light up the scoreboard, he first needs to show the coaching staff he can reliably manage a game if QB1 goes down.
“Coach McCarthy, he talks about the statistics. There’s around 36 big plays a game,” Howard said. “They’re going to come. You can’t go chasing them. The minute you go chasing them, you get in trouble. You’ve just got to be brilliant in the basics and wait for them to come.”
It could come down to a cut-down day decision to determine what’s next for this QB room. But after Friday, the picture should at least begin to come into focus.

full_text:
The Seahawks are the reigning NFC champions, but Austin Mock's NFL Projection Model doesn't see them winning the conference again this year. Ronald Martinez / Getty Images
My NFL Projection Model doubted the Seattle Seahawks last year and looked foolish. And did it learn its lesson? Nope!
While my model is projecting a far better season for Seattle than the 8.6 wins it forecast last year, it doesn’t believe the reigning Super Bowl champs are going back-to-back.
Instead, the model is hopping aboard the Los Angeles Rams bandwagon after the Seahawks’ NFC West rival made some major splashes this offseason, trading for reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and star cornerback Trent McDuffie to bolster their defense. Honestly, the model isn’t really slighting Seattle, forecasting the Seahawks to win the second-most games in the NFC and third-most in the NFL.
But that’s not to say it’s a two-horse race in the NFC. The model projects three more teams to finish with 10-plus wins, and a few more to win at least nine. So, while the NFC is not quite as wide-open as the AFC, there are still several teams with a realistic shot at making the playoffs and winning the Super Bowl.
Like we did yesterday for the AFC , let’s examine the odds before diving into each division.
Just two years ago, the Philadelphia Eagles were kings of the NFL after throttling the Kansas City Chiefs in the Super Bowl; 18 months later, their hold on the NFC East — a division they’ve won two years in a row — feels tenuous. Wide receiver A.J. Brown is gone , and while DeVonta Smith can step into his shoes as the offense’s No. 1, not having a pair of star pass catchers could be tough for Jalen Hurts.
If the Eagles’ quarterback struggles again this season, real questions will be asked about his future as the franchise’s starting quarterback. Perhaps a change at offensive coordinator — Hurts is used to those by now — will help the QB return to form. Even though Sean Mannion is young and inexperienced, my model thinks he’ll spark the offense. And even if it doesn’t, the defense has a chance to be elite again, which gives Philly a leg up to win this division for a third straight time.
The Dallas Cowboys are the NFC’s Cincinnati Bengals. And by that, I mean the model is confident the offense will be great, but the defense is a much bigger question. The Cowboys’ defense improved in the second half of last season after the team traded for defensive tackle Quinnen Williams; they’ve since added pass rushers Rashan Gary (trade), Von Miller (free agency) and Malachi Lawrence (first round of the draft) to form a potentially formidable front alongside Donovan Ezeiruaku. And, of course, the Cowboys spent their other first-round pick on do-it-all defensive back Caleb Downs. If the young players can thrive in a system that revolves around Williams and boost Dallas’ defense, that will give QB Dak Prescott and company a high ceiling.
The Washington Commanders and New York Giants aren’t hopeless, but the model sees their rosters as significantly weaker than those of the Eagles and Cowboys. Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels and New York’s Jaxson Dart must stay healthy and take the next step for either of these teams to be contenders. Washington added a handful of solid veterans in free agency to bolster the defense, so that will be worth monitoring. As for the Giants, can new head coach John Harbaugh raise this team’s floor ? If so, how high?
The model is calling its worst-to-first shot right here. The Detroit Lions finished last in the NFC North last year at 9-8, but my model sees them as the favorites this year, and that’s primarily because of a favorable schedule. Per my model, the Lions play the 29th-easiest schedule in the league, which is expected to give them an extra half win over their rivals.
The Green Bay Packers are perhaps the toughest team to project this year, with a wide range of possible outcomes. Star pass rusher Micah Parsons will be out for at least the first month of the season. Without him last year, the Packers ranked 28th in EPA per play; they were 15th with him on the field. I like new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon, but is there enough for him to work with? A similar question could be asked for coach Matt LaFleur’s offense . He’s good, but there are some major issues on that offensive line, and I could see the bottom falling out for this offense if QB Jordan Love lacks adequate protection.
The NFC North is tricky! The Chicago Bears are another team that’s tough to decipher. All eyes are on Caleb Williams and whether he can improve his down-to-down consistency this season. Yes, the Bears won the division in 2025, but Williams finished outside the top 20 in dropback EPA and dropback success rate. If that doesn’t improve, I have little faith in a defense that’s likely to take a step back after relying heavily on creating turnovers last year.
The Minnesota Vikings are projected to finish last, but they are getting a big upgrade at quarterback with Kyler Murray. I’m not sure if Murray is a top-10 quarterback, but I’m confident he can play at that level for stretches, even if he ends up being closer to average. That’s still a huge improvement over what they got from their quarterbacks last year. Pair average quarterback play with those receivers and defensive coordinator Brian Flores, and you’re going to find yourself in the playoff hunt more often than not.
An 8-9 record topped the NFC South last year, and my model forecasts a similar outcome this year, with no team in the division projected to win more than eight games.
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are favored to win the division, but they’re old, and their quarterback, Baker Mayfield, is unhappy that he hasn’t signed an extension yet. Perhaps Mayfield will use that as motivation and deliver a big season. If he doesn’t, though, maybe he’s not Tampa’s QB next season. Meanwhile, the New Orleans Saints are right behind them, but they just lost their first-round wide receiver Jordyn Tyson to another hamstring injury, so he’s going on the shelf for a bit. New Orleans also lost underrated defensive tackle Bryan Bresee earlier in camp.
The Atlanta Falcons already look like they’re in trouble at QB , as Michael Penix Jr. doesn’t look like he’ll be ready for the start of the season and there are now questions about Tua Tagovailoa’s health for Week 1. Yes, Bijan Robinson, Drake London and Kyle Pitts are an awesome trio of playmakers, but if no one can get them the ball consistently, how much can they do?
And then there’s the first-to-worst Carolina Panthers. That’s right, a year after they “conquered” the division at 8-9, my model forecasts a division-worst 6.7 wins for the Panthers in 2026. That’s partially because of a difficult schedule, but mostly because the model isn’t a fan of quarterback Bryce Young, especially if his offensive line isn’t healthy. Remember, they lost left tackle Ikem Ekwonu to a knee injury late last year, and right tackle Taylor Moton is out for an extended period with a blood clot in his lung.
My model already loved the Rams, so it’s no surprise that after adding Garrett and McDuffie, Los Angeles is projected to be the best team in the NFL. But even being the odds-on favorite this season only gives them a 14 percent chance to win the Super Bowl, as they play in an incredibly tough division and have the league’s third-toughest schedule.
The Seahawks look to repeat as Super Bowl champions, and if they do, we’ll start having serious conversations about head coach Mike Macdonald and his place in history (the next Bill Belichick?). If he can keep this defense elite after losing some key players in free agency, it will be impressive. My bigger concerns for Seattle, however, come on offense. Former offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak left to become head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders, and the Seahawks are turning over play-calling duties to an unknown commodity in Brian Fleury. title: Cardinals Rookie Has Stunning Chance to Return to College Football
full_text:
ARIZONA — In an odd turn of events, the Arizona Cardinals have a rookie that might be heading back to school.
Safety Wydett Williams was one of many college football players who were granted a temporary restraining order to play one more season at the NCAA level.
Former Ole Miss starters Dae'Quan Wright, Zxavian Harris and Wydett Williams, all of whom signed with NFL teams this summer, are among a group of athletes who were granted a temporary restraining order Wednesday to return to college for one more season. https://t.co/c1oVqqt55o
According to ESPN, a total of 16 players were listed in the lawsuit. The NCAA could potentially appeal the decision.
"Those players have expressed an interest in being released from their NFL contracts, according to attorney Ryan Downton, and if their NFL teams release them by Sept. 1 they will be allowed to join a college roster under the restraining order," said ESPN in their story .
The NCAA recently reworked its eligibility rules to allow five seasons to be played in five years, as opposed to four seasons. The Division I board of directors opted to not include recent seniors — which Williams was part of.
"NCAA officials said they did not want a sudden influx of returning fifth-year players to take roster spots from incoming freshmen, many of whom had already signed on to play for their teams by the time the rule was changed," ESPN continued.
"That decision prompted the current wave of lawsuits that have come through state and federal courts. In several cases, judges have granted temporary restraining orders that allow athletes to compete in the upcoming season while their case is pending."
Williams, listed at 6-1 and 200 lbs on his scouting profile, began his college career at Delta State before transferring to Louisiana-Monroe (2024) and Ole Miss (2025) before going undrafted this past spring.
Williams is not currently projected to make the Cardinals' 53-man roster but could end up on a practice squad. After going undrafted, perhaps Williams feels like he could improve his game and change his fate by the 2027 NFL Draft.
If he does depart, Williams will likely transfer to a different school that failed to supplement their safety position through either recruiting or the transfer portal.
NFL rosters are due to be cut down from 90 to 53 on Sunday, Aug. 30. Players released are subject to waivers, where other teams can add them to their roster/practice squad.
With Budda Baker, Andrew Wingard, Dadrion Taylor-Demerson and Kitan Crawford already on the roster, the Cardinals' safety room is fairly full — which will likely see Williams off the team.
Williams has nine total tackles across Arizona's two preseason games.

title: Cardinals Can Copy Jaguars' Miracle Turnaround — Andrew Wingard Has Been Here Before
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are hoping for an eye-opening turnaround in 2026.
An organization that's won just a combined 15 games in the last three seasons is hoping new head coach Mike LaFleur can turn the tide in the desert. So far, there's hope of that happening thanks to an improved offensive attack while the defense remains to be seen.
If there's a player who knows anything about bad football teams flipping a switch, it's new safety Andrew Wingard.
Wingard, who signed this offseason as a free agent, played seven years with the Jacksonville Jaguars. In his first three years (2019-21) with the Jaguars, Jacksonville won a combined ten games. Last season, the Jaguars won the division with a 13-4 record.
After watching Coen (a Sean McVay coaching tree disciple) turn things around in Duval, Wingard will be one of many chess pieces hoping to help another McVay product in LaFleur replicate the same success.
"I am," Wingard told reporters when asked if he's seeing shades of similar building blocks.
"In the locker room, it just takes ball players, and that's all you can focus on. I've loved every second of it since I've stepped in this building and in this locker room. I haven't seen a single ego. There's no divas. It's like all these guys are such good guys and good people, and that was one of our things in Jacksonville that got us over the top. We just had dudes that cared about each other and were good people and go to work every day and grind. So I've seen nothing but great things from all these guys since I stepped in the building and they've welcomed me in, and it's felt great."
Often times it can be tricky for a first-year coach to take command of a locker room. LaFleur, an exciting but massively unproven hire, has impressed according to Wingard.
"He's been awesome. First day of OTAs, he commands it, and it's not the sort of like, he walks in and it's the drill sergeant sort of command. He's cool, he's relaxed. He's just a good dude. But he commands it, and he's funny. Like he's a funny dude, and guys buy into that," said Wingard.
"But you can tell he has command on the side. And obviously his track record speaks for itself. He's had nothing but success wherever he's been, and he's freaking smart. We get into these walkthroughs, and he'll pause the drill and start talking to the offense, and I'm just like, 'damn, this guy knows his sh--.' But he's impressive."
The Cardinals are widely being overlooked ahead of 2026. A first-year coach, no established franchise quarterback, playing in the NFC West with one of the league's toughest schedules will certainly do that.
That's life, but also life in the NFL offers parity. Over 60% of games come down to one score, and there's just a dash of hope LaFleur will have the Cardinals in more games than they were last season.
The games will trickle in one Sunday at a time, though the most important ingredient to success is players buying in together — which Wingard believes is present in Arizona.
"It's honestly one of the coolest locker rooms I've ever been in. Like everyone is just so cool, truly cool as hell. Like all the guys are real authentic. So I think that's been the biggest thing. And when you're that close with people, it makes playing with each other a lot more fun," he said.
"I've been on teams where you go out on Sunday and you feel like you're out there by yourself. That's not fun, and that doesn't make you feel good, nor does it make you play good. And some of the best teams I've been on have been the coolest dudes I've been with, and you're out there and you feel like you're in college again because you grind with these guys.
"You talk to these guys, you care about these guys, and when we go out there and practice, it's fun because we care about each other, and it's fun to play with guys you care about, and that only just feeds into the beast even more."

title: Cardinals Mailbag: Carson Beck Prediction, Tough Roster Decisions Looming and More
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are halfway done with their preseason slate.
Training camp, at least at State Farm Stadium, is in the books as head coach Mike LaFleur takes his operation back to Tempe for the remaining stretch. As we approach final roster cuts, each practice and game only increases with importance.
Thanks to everybody who participated in the mailbag. If you'd like to chime in for future iterations, you can drop me a follow on X here .
And to quote the great Lil Wayne: Sorry for the wait.
A: I'm not so sure, WiseOwl.
The deeper we get into the preseason, the more I'm becoming convinced the Cardinals will truly use a rotation at the other spot next to Mack Wilson depending on what the down/distance is. Simon took the majority of first-team reps since OTA's, though Gibbens' recent start in preseason keeps the door open.
Gibbens' acumen in coverage makes him an attractive nickel linebacker who can play either pass or run while Simon has the prior experience calling Nick Rallis' defense.
Much like the defensive line, the "starting" label may not carry significant weight here. The early signs are Arizona wants to deploy both .
A: Kendrick Bourne is comfortably the Cardinals' WR3, and quite honestly he's silently had an impressive camp. Bourne isn't making many headlines thanks to other stars around him, though he's seemingly always open and I can't recall a drop he's had in either training camp or preseason.
Bourne, already beloved by the locker room, fits more into that prototypical "slot" receiver role. When the Cardinals are in 11 personnel, he's typically there. Yet LaFleur's moved receivers around across the offense depending on the various goals of the play.
One thing I can say is the Cardinals have often motioned Bourne either across the formation or just inward to either crash down on blocking a front seven player or faking the block before whipping out for a route.
Bourne doesn't project to get fed consistently but he's a clear favorite of LaFleur and has been impactful when utilized.
A: KIZ, this is a pretty tough conversation the Cardinals will have to have at some point. Arizona could keep five or six receivers depending on the outlook of the roster.
Right now, it does feel like five receivers are penciled in: Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson, Kendrick Bourne, Devin Duvernay and Reggie Virgil. The top three are obvious while Duvernay is their primary return man and Virgil is a fresh draft pick who has looked fairly strong in the limited action we've seen.
If the Cardinals keep a sixth wideout, there's a plethora of guys who are performing well. Practically the entire receiving room looks strong. Right now, Jalen Brooks and Ihmir Smith-Marsette are the top two candidates battling for the WR6 spot with Simi Fehoko, Bryson Green, Xavier Weaver and Harrison Wallace all behind.
Personally, Brooks has the edge for me at this moment in time.
Lon Tay, Reiman's going to be a massive piece to their run-blocking puzzle.
When exactly he returns remains to be determined. For what it's worth he was spotted getting some side work during the open portion of practice earlier in camp but he hasn't been activated from the PUP list.
Mike LaFleur insists the PUP guys are making progress, though it's unclear exactly when the Cardinals could see their tight end back into the mix. To me, this feels like a coin flip in terms of his availability for Week 1.
We'll need to see something soon, like this week, to make us believe he can contribute and be physically ready for the season opener.
Bryan this is actually an article I plan on doing soon, but I'll give you guys a spoiler:
1. Practice times are later in the day, like much later. Gannon preferred to have practice earlier in the day while LaFleur very much adopted a later start-time approach from the likes of Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan. I'm sure there's some sports science behind it.
2. Much more 11 v 11 during practices compared to Gannon, who preferred to mix in some individual and 7 v 7. However, LaFleur's big thing is "7 v 7 is not real football" so the Cardinals have a heavy dose of team offense vs defense now.
3. The instant replay boards that show the play immediately after it happens. Gannon didn't have that at either State Farm Stadium or Tempe, whereas LaFleur has both. The Cardinals loved it and referred to the replay system as a good way to provide immediate feedback as opposed to waiting for film study.
Ed, the good part for me has been the Cardinals' offense and how often receivers are getting open. Every level (starters to third string) has found success offensively. I think that's a strong indictment on LaFleur's system and ability to scheme guys open.
Shaking my head? To be quite honest there wasn't a lot that left me shaking my head. The Josh Sweat saga has been the closest thing, though I understand the Cardinals are probably just protecting their top investment and his knee ahead of the regular season.
Charles, the recent rib injury doesn't quite impact his chances of starting in 2026, mostly because Jacoby Brissett has those duties locked — at least for the beginning stage of the season.
It does feel likely we see Beck at some point in time, barring a surprisingly competitive Cardinals campaign. The big question here is when Arizona feels the need to see Beck, as the Cardinals are well aware of the grueling schedule ahead.
I personally don't think we see Beck until halfway through the season at the earliest. Obviously, I could be wrong (just ask any of my ex's) but after handing Brissett $15 million guaranteed, they're going to want to squeeze as much juice out of him as possible.
Unofficial prediction? I'll go Week 12 vs. Washington. That would give him two games before their bye week to regroup and assess Beck before the final four games of the season. The Cardinals just might be out of playoff contention by then, too.
Frankie, we sort of touched on this a bit earlier, but Jalen Brooks' rise from the bottom of the depth chart to a very real possibility of making the roster has been notable. He's somebody I'm watching with intrigue because it's not a clear-cut winning battle due to either numbers or competition.
Jayden Williams' ascension through camp has been super fun to watch. It's not often a seventh-round pick climbs his way to potential swing-tackle duties over the course of a summer, but the Ole Miss product has legitimately been that impressive. He's still developing, but the Cardinals seem to really like him.
Eku Leota and Bam Knight are other guys who might've been on the outside looking in entering camp with strong chances of making the team.
